 BALTIMORE (WBFF) — Fresh off election victories that gave Democrats control of Congress, Maryland lawmakers are preparing to reverse cuts to federal food assistance as the Trump administration says it has uncovered billions of dollars in fraud involving the program.
 The political showdown puts President Donald Trump's signature domestic legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill, back in the crosshairs, with Democrats arguing voters have given them a mandate for change and Republicans defending the cuts as necessary to protect taxpayers and prevent abuse.
 But Trump, who retains veto power despite the shift in congressional control, isn't saying whether he would sign legislation restoring the benefits or block Democrats' efforts.
 The White House did not directly answer Spotlight on Maryland's question about whether the president would sign or veto legislation reversing the cuts.
 The stakes extend beyond Washington, D.C.
 In Maryland, nearly 36,000 residents have lost SNAP. That includes Rhonda Harris, a disabled Baltimore resident who said her benefits keep getting cut.
 “First it was $16, then it was another $20," she said.
 Harris receives about $270 every month to help pay for groceries and also relies on Baltimore-area food pantries to help fill the gaps. She said every dollar matters, and she has a child, her mother, and two dogs to care for.
 “I’m already below the poverty line,” she said.
 The SNAP program provides food assistance to low-income individuals and families. She also relies on local food pantries to help fill the gaps.
 “With prices going up and the benefits going down, it’s sometimes hard to manage,” Harris said.
 Maryland Democrats in Congress are preparing to push for a reversal on SNAP cuts.
 Nine of Maryland’s 10 congressional members are Democrats. U.S. Rep. Johnny Olszewski, a Baltimore County Democrat, told Spotlight on Maryland he expects to help introduce legislation to restore the cuts under the new Congress. Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks also support reversing the changes.
 The state’s lone Republican congressman, Andy Harris, defended the SNAP cuts, telling Spotlight in a statement they are intended to reduce waste, fraud and abuse while ensuring eligible Marylanders can still receive benefits.
 Flavio Hickel, a political science professor at Washington College, said he doubts Trump would sign a bill reversing a major part of his legislative agenda.
 “I think he is probably loath to do anything that could tinker with the legacy of the Big Beautiful Bill,” Hickel said. “On the other hand, Trump is very unpredictable.”
 Billions in fraud 
 The Trump administration has defended the changes, telling Spotlight on Maryland the president’s legislation “began the process to halt fraud and ensure it only serves eligible Americans Rather than throwing money at a broken system, the Trump Administration will continue to stop fraudsters stealing from these important programs, as well as take effective, cost-saving steps to make life more affordable for all Americans.”
 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins has said federal officials uncovered nearly $10 billion in fraud and made approximately 1,000 arrests.
 The Justice Department also recently announced a nationwide enforcement operation targeting SNAP fraud involving more than 40 defendants and nearly $42 million in alleged or proven fraudulent activity.
 The cases included schemes involving stolen benefit cards, fraudulent transactions and retailers accused of illegally exchanging benefits for cash.
 Federal prosecutors in Maryland have signaled that additional cases could be coming.
 Kelly Hayes, the U.S. attorney for the District of Maryland, told Spotlight last month that investigators are continuing to uncover fraud and intend to make SNAP a significant enforcement priority.
 “I think we’re just seeing the tip of the iceberg. We’re continuing to unravel all of these,” Hayes said.
 'This is unstable' 
 Even if Democrats succeed in restoring the benefits, Hickel said the debate over food assistance points to a larger concern about the uncertainty families face when federal policies change. There's also a lingering question of whether each major political party will try to undo the other's work when power shifts.
 “There is this fear that this is unstable, that it could change in a couple of years,” Hickel said. “That lack of predictability creates tremendous anxiety in your sort of lived experience, in your planning over the long term, months and years and that sort of thing.”
 Hickel said Democrats need to do more than simply restore previous policies. He said they should work toward creating programs with broader support that can withstand changes in political leadership.
 “I think they need to try and build something new that has broad-based support," he said.
 Hickel also warned that changes in federal funding could put additional financial pressure on states like Maryland to cover more of the cost of food assistance programs.
 That could create new challenges for an already strained state budget, and tax increases remain a possibility.
 For Rhonda Harris, the political debate is secondary to the immediate challenge of putting food on the table.
 “Every little bit helps,” she said.
